meaning.evidence: The agency's name is corrupted: "U.S. Tucker and Drug Administration". A reader would not know which body keeps the flush list. Everything else is the original verbatim.

sense.evidence: "Tucker" replaces the "Food" in a proper noun, which is badly wrong sense. "dunny" fits. "heaps of the medicine remains" is fine in sense but ungrammatical.

authenticity.evidence: The few swaps are mechanical, and the original's own slips stay ("Drop off them", "To discard of"). Barely any Aussie to judge, and what is there includes a pastiche error.

register.evidence: Almost untranslated: only "dunny", "heaps" and "authorised" change. Well short of level 2.

tone.evidence: Still reads as sober health guidance, but "Tucker and Drug Administration" gives an unintended comic note.

flow.evidence: Readable as the original is, but "Drop off them" and "heaps of the medicine remains" jar.

variety.evidence: Too little slang to vary. "dunny" twice.

essence.evidence: Recognisably the FDA page, with the agency-name error.

problems.why: It translates "Food" inside an agency's proper name, so it names a body that does not exist.

problems.original: a lot of the medicine remains

problems.quote: Drop off them at a drug take-back location.
problems.original: Drop off them at a drug take-back location.
problems.why: Left untranslated, including the original's ungrammatical wording. Representative of the whole text sitting below the brief.

A.summary: Essentially untranslated, with one critical mistranslation of the agency's name.

meaning.evidence: Every instruction survives in order, with accurate localisation: "Check with your local police", "chemists", "household rubbish bin", "Post the envelope".

sense.evidence: All terms fit: "chockers", "kitty litter", "rummaging through the bin", "Chuck the container in the bin".

authenticity.evidence: Reads like an Australian government health page: "Some pharmacies give them out for free", "isn't handy".

register.evidence: A light level-2 touch, mostly vocabulary (chockers, chemists, rubbish, chuck), with sober guidance kept and no swearing.

tone.evidence: Stays calm and instructional, and the fentanyl warning stays serious: "can be dangerous to people it's not prescribed for".

flow.evidence: Smooth plain English: "Take the drugs out of their original containers and mix them with something unpleasant".

variety.evidence: Fine for its weight, but "get rid of" is used for every disposal verb and "isn't handy" appears twice.

problems.quote: To get rid of your prescription or over-the-counter medicines
problems.original: To discard of your prescription or over-the-counter medicines
problems.why: "Get rid of" recurs for nearly every disposal verb.

B.summary: An accurate, light, natural level-2 localisation that keeps the guidance sober.

meaning.evidence: All the steps survive. "ask your doctor or your chemist" narrows "health care professional" slightly, and "Then bin the packaging" is fine.

sense.evidence: Terms fit their contexts: "have a squiz at the list", "chockers", "Chuck the container in the bin". "something yucky" fits "undesirable" loosely.

authenticity.evidence: Natural Australian voice: "meds", "have a squiz", "Some chemists hand them out for free".

register.evidence: A bit above a light touch for official health guidance: "dunny" twice, "have a squiz", "yucky" and "here's what to do" push towards level 3.

tone.evidence: Mostly sober, but "something yucky" and "the dunny" lighten a public-safety text a little.

flow.evidence: Smooth, conversational and easy to follow: "If neither of those works for you, here's what to do".

variety.evidence: More varied in openers and terms, but "handy" appears three times ("no take-back option handy").

essence.evidence: Clearly the FDA guidance, all points intact.

problems.why: Childish register for a safety instruction.

problems.quote: When there's no take-back option handy
problems.original: When a take-back option is not easily available

problems.quote: flush these potentially dangerous medicines down the dunny
problems.original: flush these potentially dangerous medicines down the toilet
problems.why: "Dunny" in official safety guidance nudges past a light touch.

C.summary: A fluent, natural version, a shade chattier than level 2 asks for in a safety text.
